## Spatial & Geometric Definition
* Geometry Type: Polygon (Flow_Structure_Polygon).

* Spatial Delineation: 3D structural stone footprint resting on the riverbed, representing river training dikes, chevrons, bendway weirs, closing dams, and hard-points.

* Structural Material: 100% quarried limestone/dolomite riprap and stone core.

### Primary Restoration & Engineering Objectives
* Channel Steering & Velocity Partitioning: Direct river discharge into primary navigation lines while partitioning secondary flows into restoration backwaters.

* Scour Hole Generation: Carve deep structural aquatic habitat niches through localized flow acceleration around structure tips and heads.

* Island & Shoreline Sheltering: Act as rigid upstream hydrodynamic deflection shields protecting soft downstream wetland deposits.

### Typical Cross-Sections, Dimensions & Sizing Criteria
* Crest Widths: 6.0 to 12.0 ft along the top weir crest.

* Side Slopes: Heavy stable stone slopes of 1V:1.5H to 1V:2H.

* Crest Elevation: Range from submerged low sills (1.0 to 3.0 ft below pool) up to emergent structures (2.0 to 5.0 ft above normal pool).

* Structural Prow / Nose: Heavily reinforced rounded apex with stone sizing upgraded to Class V (d 50 ≥24 in) to withstand direct river ice sheets.

### Construction & Implementation Methodology
* Marine Derrick Operations: Heavy rock barges positioned with tugboats; stone placed using clamshell buckets or hydraulic excavators working against river currents.

* Upstream Root Tie-In: Structure landward roots deeply keyed into adjacent banks (15 to 30 ft) to prevent high-water flanking.

### Quality Control, Inspection & Long-Term Maintenance
* Acoustic Bathymetric Scans: Side-scan and multi-beam hydrographic surveys monitoring bed scour development and verifying structural mass stability.

## Spatial Feature Attributes
### Definition
River Flow Structure polygon is a natural or man-made flow (or sediment) control structure in a water course or water body such as a dike or weir. This feature should not be used to model a levee. The polygon feature class is for features large enough that a polygon can be drawn around them and reasonably seen at a project-level extent.

### Purpose
Riverine flow structures, also called "river training structures," are man-made constructions designed to modify the flow of a river, typically to control erosion, manage sediment transport, improve navigation, protect riverbanks, and sometimes enhance aquatic habitats by influencing water flow dynamics within the river channel.

### Applicability
Training structures can be used to alter hydrodynamic conditions, the sediment transport regime, and ultimately habitat conditions on the UMRS. The 2010 EMP Report to Congress described how river training structures meet UMRS Environmental Objectives by improving fish habitat and water quality, stabilizing eroding channels, reducing sediment load to backwaters by reducing flow velocities, and maintaining water temperature and rock substrate. (UMRR Design Handbook, 2012)

### Notes
Restoration features now have a Program_UID field to distinguish between NESP and UMRR features. Aliases without program identification will be created for any field that currently has UMRR in the name, so they can be used for NESP or UMRR data.

Attribute criteria for each field includes the following:

* Attribute Status – defines whether the field requires a value or if it is optional based on available information.
* Phases – indicates the earliest time in the project lifecycle values for this attribute are available.
* Digitizing requirements – indicates when the field value should be entered in the attribute table.

Geometry Note: Points should have well top elevation as Z value if available.

### RiverineFlowStructure
(polygon) – A natural or man-made flow (or sediment) control structure in a water course or water body such as a dike or weir. This feature should be used to represent the footprint of the feature.

## Parameters

### Program_UID
Designate program NESP or UMRR.

### Project_ID (alias: PROJECT_ID)
Foreign key to the unique NESP/UMRR project ID.

### Type (alias)
A broad classification used to group NESP/UMRR restoration features into categories of similar function.

<table class="table-grid">
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>Value</th>
      <th>Description</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Shoreline Protection</td>
      <td>Measures taken to reduce erosion from banks and islands due to wind, wave, and ice action.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Channel Modifications</td>
      <td>Measures taken to train the main channel of a river and to modify secondary channels.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

### SubType (alias: Subtype)
A classification used to group NESP/UMRR restoration features into specific design feature categories.

<table class="table-grid">
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>Value</th>
      <th>Description</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Rock groin</td>
      <td>Placement of rock extending from shore into shallow water, perpendicular to shore. Encourages deposition of sediment along the groin and erosion between groins to form stable scallop shapes; appropriate where wave action and littoral drift are dominant processes.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Rock vane</td>
      <td>Placement of rock extending from shore into water at 45–60 degrees upstream, away from shore; features a sloping top and directs current away from shore; can also reduce littoral drift.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>J-hook vane</td>
      <td>Rock vane with a “J”-shaped hook whose outside curve faces upstream.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Cross vane</td>
      <td>U-shaped vane keyed into both banklines and sloping down to the top of the U pointing upstream; used to offset adverse effects of straight weirs and check dams.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Root-wad vane</td>
      <td>Placement of root wads extending from shore into water at 45–60 degrees upstream, away from shore.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Spur dike</td>
      <td>Series of river training structures perpendicular to shore used to establish normal channel width, direct flow, promote scour and deposition, and trap bedload to build banks.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>L-head dike</td>
      <td>Training dike with a perpendicular dike structure attached at the channel end (shoreward), forming an “L” shape to control scour patterns at the riverward end.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Alternating dike</td>
      <td>Structures constructed in straight side channels to encourage development of sinuous flow.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Stepped-up dike</td>
      <td>Field of dikes that increase in elevation (generally ~2 ft dike-to-dike) to change morphology of natural alluvial waterways.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Chevron dike</td>
      <td>V- or U-shaped rock dike pointing upstream and unattached to bankline, typically built above flat-pool elevation to ~2-year flood elevation; used in wide reaches to split flow and enhance habitat and to provide dredged-material placement area.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Longitudinal peak stone toe</td>
      <td>Continuous stone dike keyed into bank at upstream and downstream ends, placed at the toe of an eroding bend bankline; can be offset from bank to smooth alignment through a bend.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Bendway weir</td>
      <td>Low-level, completely submerged rock structure placed on the outside bankline of a bend and angled upstream toward flow, extending into the navigation channel; prevents excess deepening and reduces outside-bank erosion.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>W-weir</td>
      <td>W-shaped rock structure in the channel, center of W facing downstream; ends tied into bank at bankfull elevation; slopes down to two upstream points and up slightly to center; provides bed control and enhanced fish habitat.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Closure structure</td>
      <td>Rock, earth, or wood structures constructed across secondary channels to reduce floodplain conveyance and increase main channel depths; may be submerged or emerged.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Rock-Log structure</td>
      <td>Economical alternative to offshore rock mounds where ice impacts are minimal; logs anchored at both ends by rock.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Wood pile structure</td>
      <td>Logs driven into the river bed to create roughness and form river training structures, benefiting macro- and microinvertebrates.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Offshore rock mounds</td>
      <td>Rock placed offshore from shorelines where shoreline protection is needed, particularly where nearshore bathymetry is shallow, shorelines are poorly defined, or direct rock placement is difficult.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Boulder clusters</td>
      <td>Large stones placed slightly below base-flow water surface elevation to diversify flow regime and provide in-channel refuges.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Multiple round points</td>
      <td>Field of round stone structures, generally slightly emerged, used to create bathymetric and flow diversity.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Side channel hard point</td>
      <td>Stone structures placed at regular intervals along an eroding bank, trenched, keyed, or dumped on shore to resist forces associated with bank failure.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Woody debris</td>
      <td>Trees at least 25 ft long placed perpendicular or at an angle to shoreline; trunks may be buried or rock-keyed, typically in wave-sheltered areas.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Spillway</td>
      <td>Section of embankment engineered to provide controlled overtopping of an embankment system, typically at the downstream end at a lower elevation than the exterior berm.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Diversion</td>
      <td>Structure intended to divert flow from the main channel, typically into a bypass or cut-off channel.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Other</td>
      <td>Other type of riverine flow structure; must be specified in sdsFeatureDescription.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
